source_questions: A sample of water on analysis has been found to maintain the following in gm/L. Ca (HCO3)2 = 4.86, Mg (HCO3)2 = 5.84, CaSO4 = 6.80, MgSO4 = 8.40. Calculate the temporary and permanent hardness of water in degree French & degree Clarke.

Calculate the temporary and permanent hardness of water sample having the following salts. Ca (HCO3)2 = 162 mg/L, Mg (HCO3)2 = 73 mg/L, CaSO4 = 136 mg/L, MgCl2 = 95 mg/L, CaCl2 = 111 mg/L, NaCl= 100 mg/L, Suspended matter = 50 mg/L.

Determine the total hardness of a sample of water in degree French & degree Clarke, which showed the following analysis: MgCl2 = 19 ppm, MgSO4 = 12 ppm, Ca(NO3)2= 16.4 ppm, NaOH = 40ppm, KOH = 56 ppm,  suspended matter= 100 ppm, Ca (HCO3)2 = 162 ppm and Mg(NO3)2 =14.8 ppm.

Calculate the temporary and permanent hardness of water in ppm, degree French & degree Clarke of a sample of water containing the following dissolved salts. CaCO3 = 100 mg/L, Mg (HCO3)2 = 14.6 mg/L, HCl= 36 mg/L, MgSO4 = 12 mg/L, NaCl= 84 mg/L, CaCl2 = 11.1mg/L
completion_author: PankusDesk; supplied PDF provides equivalence tables but not complete solutions for its four numbered questions.

problem_4.assumption: All listed salts, including CaCO3, contribute dissolved Ca/Mg as stated; no Ca/Mg removal by precipitation. HCl reduces carbonate alkalinity and increases non-carbonate hardness without changing total hardness.
problem_4.independent_verification: Total hardness from Ca/Mg millimoles; carbonate hardness from remaining alkalinity in milliequivalents. Both exactly agree with the salt-equivalent/acid method.
